column4:
As a 4th-year student from the old curriculum, in my perspective I’m judging based on (quality / attending one class session) and only on the knowledge gained in class, not outside the classroom. My opinions are as follows:

1. Some courses do not meet the needs of real-world work because they are outdated, such as CSC325, CSC340, and CSC319. In my view, these courses should teach more than just GUI development and restructuring. I think the content is quite old. To make Java more practically useful, it should involve building a full Desktop Application or doing a Big Data project instead.

2. Courses that should be hands-on ended up being mostly theoretical. For example, CSC220 was very disappointing for me in terms of learning networking. I believe this subject has huge potential for further development, but it felt like there was a lot of talk and not much substance. We pay almost 50,000 baht to sit in an old CB building without doing any concrete lab work, unlike other faculties that pay less but have proper networking workshops. Meanwhile, we just sit there, looking at each other, after paying tens of thousands more but receiving lower quality than other departments.

CSC325 was also disappointing. I believe this course still has potential and could offer much more. There was no project at all. Most of the time was spent grinding through SeedLab, documenting it, and then taking the final exam. In the end, there was no real continuation or application. I see this course as almost useful — it was just missing a focus on quality, as it emphasized quantity of work instead.

3. There was a gap in coding practice. During Years 1–2, it was the most stressful period, but also the most beneficial for me. However, in Years 3–4, I felt like coding almost completely disappeared. It became very theory-heavy, with not much hands-on practice. I understand that this might be due to the reasons mentioned in points 1 and 2. I also feel that this may have already been improved in the new curriculum. Overall, though, I found the learning experience enjoyable during my time here.

column4:
Language and General Education Courses (LNG and GEN): These courses are not useful and waste a lot of time. Students with very high IELTS scores still have to take basic language classes, which doesn't make sense. Additionally, the grading standards are unclear and difficult to verify.
Programming Courses: The instructors are skilled and knowledgeable, which is good. However, the courses focus too much on fundamentals and theory. The practical application is very limited. Students have to learn and adapt a lot on their own to be ready for internships.
Need for More Specialized Elective Courses: The curriculum should offer more specialized track options. For example, UX/UI in course 105 could be a full elective course, but currently it only covers basic concepts that cannot be applied in real work. We would like to see courses such as Game Development with Unity, Advanced Power BI for Data Science
Other industry-relevant specialized topics
Courses 100/101 (Coursera ), 301, and 302: These courses waste time and do not measure any real CS skills or abilities. I don't understand the purpose of having them except to take time away from more necessary work.

column4:
Most of the courses were quite helpful. To name a few:
CSC209 Data Structures: While the sessions occasionally ran longer than scheduled, the content and the instructor were excellent. The instructor explained concepts clearly with ample examples. Although class times were sometimes flexible due to his responsibilities as the Department Dean, the material remained highly practical and valuable.
CSC105 Web Application Development: Some students felt this course only covered the basics, but I personally appreciated the approach. It encourages "learning how to learn." Instead of just following instructions, we were pushed to think for ourselves. This is essential for developing the skills needed to form original ideas and manage our own projects.
Overall, I think a score of 4 is appropriate, as the quality of the class is great but there is still room for improvement.

I got really high English test score. I really don’t understand why, us as an international program students, have to learn such a basic English concept of an elementary school grader level? Not only it’s not useful it’s also waste of my time and energy to attend all those courses In Jarah course, I don’t understand why LINE is consistently used as the main communication channel for assignments, class materials, and important course details. LINE has limited message history accessibility and is not a professional or reliable platform for managing academic information.
Using LINE for quick reminders or minor announcements is acceptable. But relying on it for all course-related communication is excessive and problematic. The faculty already provides proper platforms such as Microsoft Teams and CSCMS, which are designed for structured communication, assignment posting, and long-term record keeping.
Because information is frequently shared only through LINE chats, important details are often missed or lost, leading to confusion among students. Assignments communicated verbally in class, through chat messages, or by asking students to take notes are subjective and lack clarity. As a result, many students are uncertain about task requirements, deadlines, and expectations.
Assignments and course materials should be consistently posted on Microsoft Teams or CSCMS in a clear, concrete, and centralized manner. This would significantly reduce misunderstandings and help students manage their work more effectively.

This happens regularly and has caused problems for students many times. We suggest creating a better communication system where students can submit requests and track their status more easily.

- Students who are close to P'DJ get special treatment, such as being excused for late attendance or receiving other advantages.
- P'DJ's position is unclear. Sometimes acting like a senior student, sometimes like a professor. This creates tension during activities. The commanding and controlling behavior feels more like a dictator than a teacher. P'Jo has a similar position but never creates these problems or makes students feel uncomfortable. suggesting that P'DJ should receive training on professional conduct and learn to treat all students fairly and respectfully. The current situation affects the learning environment negatively.

column4:
Important academic and opportunity-related information does not always reach Burmese students (or other international students) in a timely or clear manner. For example, information about the Taiwan internship or related programs was not well communicated, while students from other international majors had already been preparing since the previous semester. This information gap creates inequality in access to opportunities and leaves students unsure about whom to contact for guidance or clarification.
I hope the SIT International Relations office can be more proactive in sharing information about exchange programs and overseas internships. The Faculty of Engineering and Science has its own International Affairs office, which is very active in regularly posting and announcing overseas opportunities. In comparison, SIT IR has been relatively quiet, and some students are not even aware that the office exists.
If workload or capacity is an issue, perhaps the university could consider hiring additional staff or involving student assistants to help with outreach and communication.

column4:
As a 4th-year student from the old curriculum, in my perspective I’m judging based on (quality / attending one class session) and only on the knowledge gained in class, not outside the classroom. My opinions are as follows:

1. Some courses do not meet the needs of real-world work because they are outdated, such as CSC325, CSC340, and CSC319. In my view, these courses should teach more than just GUI development and restructuring. I think the content is quite old. To make Java more practically useful, it should involve building a full Desktop Application or doing a Big Data project instead.

2. Courses that should be hands-on ended up being mostly theoretical. For example, CSC220 was very disappointing for me in terms of learning networking. I believe this subject has huge potential for further development, but it felt like there was a lot of talk and not much substance. We pay almost 50,000 baht to sit in an old CB building without doing any concrete lab work, unlike other faculties that pay less but have proper networking workshops. Meanwhile, we just sit there, looking at each other, after paying tens of thousands more but receiving lower quality than other departments.

CSC325 was also disappointing. I believe this course still has potential and could offer much more. There was no project at all. Most of the time was spent grinding through SeedLab, documenting it, and then taking the final exam. In the end, there was no real continuation or application. I see this course as almost useful — it was just missing a focus on quality, as it emphasized quantity of work instead.

3. There was a gap in coding practice. During Years 1–2, it was the most stressful period, but also the most beneficial for me. However, in Years 3–4, I felt like coding almost completely disappeared. It became very theory-heavy, with not much hands-on practice. I understand that this might be due to the reasons mentioned in points 1 and 2. I also feel that this may have already been improved in the new curriculum. Overall, though, I found the learning experience enjoyable during my time here.

column4:
Language and General Education Courses (LNG and GEN): These courses are not useful and waste a lot of time. Students with very high IELTS scores still have to take basic language classes, which doesn't make sense. Additionally, the grading standards are unclear and difficult to verify.
Programming Courses: The instructors are skilled and knowledgeable, which is good. However, the courses focus too much on fundamentals and theory. The practical application is very limited. Students have to learn and adapt a lot on their own to be ready for internships.
Need for More Specialized Elective Courses: The curriculum should offer more specialized track options. For example, UX/UI in course 105 could be a full elective course, but currently it only covers basic concepts that cannot be applied in real work. We would like to see courses such as Game Development with Unity, Advanced Power BI for Data Science
Other industry-relevant specialized topics
Courses 100/101 (Coursera ), 301, and 302: These courses waste time and do not measure any real CS skills or abilities. I don't understand the purpose of having them except to take time away from more necessary work.
column6: I think Language and General Education Courses (LNG and GEN) are not useful and waste a lot of time, especially for students with high IELTS scores who still have to take basic language classes.

Most of the courses were quite helpful. To name a few:
CSC209 Data Structures: While the sessions occasionally ran longer than scheduled, the content and the instructor were excellent. The instructor explained concepts clearly with ample examples. Although class times were sometimes flexible due to his responsibilities as the Department Dean, the material remained highly practical and valuable.
CSC105 Web Application Development: Some students felt this course only covered the basics, but I personally appreciated the approach. It encourages "learning how to learn." Instead of just following instructions, we were pushed to think for ourselves. This is essential for developing the skills needed to form original ideas and manage our own projects.
Overall, I think a score of 4 is appropriate, as the quality of the class is great but there is still room for improvement.
column6: I appreciated the approach in CSC105 Web Application Development, which encourages 'learning how to learn' and pushes students to think for themselves.

I got really high English test score. I really don’t understand why, us as an international program students, have to learn such a basic English concept of an elementary school grader level? Not only it’s not useful it’s also waste of my time and energy to attend all those courses In Jarah course, I don’t understand why LINE is consistently used as the main communication channel for assignments, class materials, and important course details. LINE has limited message history accessibility and is not a professional or reliable platform for managing academic information.
Using LINE for quick reminders or minor announcements is acceptable. But relying on it for all course-related communication is excessive and problematic. The faculty already provides proper platforms such as Microsoft Teams and CSCMS, which are designed for structured communication, assignment posting, and long-term record keeping.
Because information is frequently shared only through LINE chats, important details are often missed or lost, leading to confusion among students. Assignments communicated verbally in class, through chat messages, or by asking students to take notes are subjective and lack clarity. As a result, many students are uncertain about task requirements, deadlines, and expectations.
Assignments and course materials should be consistently posted on Microsoft Teams or CSCMS in a clear, concrete, and centralized manner. This would significantly reduce misunderstandings and help students manage their work more effectively.
column6: I don't understand why, as an international program student, I have to learn basic English concepts at an elementary school level.

I understand that P'Nick has a heavy workload, but leaving students' messages on read is not acceptable, especially for urgent matters. This happens regularly and has caused problems for students many times. We suggest creating a better communication system where students can submit requests and track their status more easily.

- Unequal treatment, Female students and Thai students receive better treatment and more attention, which makes other students uncomfortable. most importantly, the clear pattern of flirting with his students is completely unacceptable and must be stopped immediately.
- Students who are close to P'DJ get special treatment, such as being excused for late attendance or receiving other advantages.
- P'DJ's position is unclear. Sometimes acting like a senior student, sometimes like a professor. This creates tension during activities. The commanding and controlling behavior feels more like a dictator than a teacher. P'Jo has a similar position but never creates these problems or makes students feel uncomfortable. suggesting that P'DJ should receive training on professional conduct and learn to treat all students fairly and respectfully. The current situation affects the learning environment negatively.

column4:
Important academic and opportunity-related information does not always reach Burmese students (or other international students) in a timely or clear manner. For example, information about the Taiwan internship or related programs was not well communicated, while students from other international majors had already been preparing since the previous semester. This information gap creates inequality in access to opportunities and leaves students unsure about whom to contact for guidance or clarification.
I hope the SIT International Relations office can be more proactive in sharing information about exchange programs and overseas internships. The Faculty of Engineering and Science has its own International Affairs office, which is very active in regularly posting and announcing overseas opportunities. In comparison, SIT IR has been relatively quiet, and some students are not even aware that the office exists.
If workload or capacity is an issue, perhaps the university could consider hiring additional staff or involving student assistants to help with outreach and communication.

column4:
As a 4th-year student from the old curriculum, in my perspective I‚Äôm judging based on (quality / attending one class session) and only on the knowledge gained in class, not outside the classroom. My opinions are as follows:

1. Some courses do not meet the needs of real-world work because they are outdated, such as CSC325, CSC340, and CSC319. In my view, these courses should teach more than just GUI development and restructuring. I think the content is quite old. To make Java more practically useful, it should involve building a full Desktop Application or doing a Big Data project instead.

2. Courses that should be hands-on ended up being mostly theoretical. For example, CSC220 was very disappointing for me in terms of learning networking. I believe this subject has huge potential for further development, but it felt like there was a lot of talk and not much substance. We pay almost 50,000 baht to sit in an old CB building without doing any concrete lab work, unlike other faculties that pay less but have proper networking workshops. Meanwhile, we just sit there, looking at each other, after paying tens of thousands more but receiving lower quality than other departments.

CSC325 was also disappointing. I believe this course still has potential and could offer much more. There was no project at all. Most of the time was spent grinding through SeedLab, documenting it, and then taking the final exam. In the end, there was no real continuation or application. I see this course as almost useful ‚Äî it was just missing a focus on quality, as it emphasized quantity of work instead.

3. There was a gap in coding practice. During Years 1‚Äì2, it was the most stressful period, but also the most beneficial for me. However, in Years 3‚Äì4, I felt like coding almost completely disappeared. It became very theory-heavy, with not much hands-on practice. I understand that this might be due to the reasons mentioned in points 1 and 2. I also feel that this may have already been improved in the new curriculum. Overall, though, I found the learning experience enjoyable during my time here.

column4:
Language and General Education Courses (LNG and GEN): These courses are not useful and waste a lot of time. Students with very high IELTS scores still have to take basic language classes, which doesn't make sense. Additionally, the grading standards are unclear and difficult to verify.
Programming Courses: The instructors are skilled and knowledgeable, which is good. However, the courses focus too much on fundamentals and theory. The practical application is very limited. Students have to learn and adapt a lot on their own to be ready for internships.
Need for More Specialized Elective Courses: The curriculum should offer more specialized track options. For example, UX/UI in course 105 could be a full elective course, but currently it only covers basic concepts that cannot be applied in real work. We would like to see courses such as Game Development with Unity, Advanced Power BI for Data Science
Other industry-relevant specialized topics
Courses 100/101 (Coursera ), 301, and 302: These courses waste time and do not measure any real CS skills or abilities. I don't understand the purpose of having them except to take time away from more necessary work.
column6: I think Language and General Education Courses (LNG and GEN) are not useful and waste a lot of time, especially for students with high IELTS scores who still have to take basic language classes.

column4:
Most of the courses were quite helpful. To name a few:
CSC209 Data Structures: While the sessions occasionally ran longer than scheduled, the content and the instructor were excellent. The instructor explained concepts clearly with ample examples. Although class times were sometimes flexible due to his responsibilities as the Department Dean, the material remained highly practical and valuable.
CSC105 Web Application Development: Some students felt this course only covered the basics, but I personally appreciated the approach. It encourages "learning how to learn." Instead of just following instructions, we were pushed to think for ourselves. This is essential for developing the skills needed to form original ideas and manage our own projects.
Overall, I think a score of 4 is appropriate, as the quality of the class is great but there is still room for improvement.
column6: I appreciated the approach in CSC105 Web Application Development, which encourages 'learning how to learn' and pushes students to think for themselves.

I got really high English test score. I really don‚Äôt understand why, us as an international program students, have to learn such a basic English concept of an elementary school grader level? Not only it‚Äôs not useful it‚Äôs also waste of my time and energy to attend all those courses In Jarah course, I don‚Äôt understand why LINE is consistently used as the main communication channel for assignments, class materials, and important course details. LINE has limited message history accessibility and is not a professional or reliable platform for managing academic information.
Using LINE for quick reminders or minor announcements is acceptable. But relying on it for all course-related communication is excessive and problematic. The faculty already provides proper platforms such as Microsoft Teams and CSCMS, which are designed for structured communication, assignment posting, and long-term record keeping.
Because information is frequently shared only through LINE chats, important details are often missed or lost, leading to confusion among students. Assignments communicated verbally in class, through chat messages, or by asking students to take notes are subjective and lack clarity. As a result, many students are uncertain about task requirements, deadlines, and expectations.
Assignments and course materials should be consistently posted on Microsoft Teams or CSCMS in a clear, concrete, and centralized manner. This would significantly reduce misunderstandings and help students manage their work more effectively.
column6: I don't understand why, as an international program student, I have to learn basic English concepts at an elementary school level.

I understand that P'Nick has a heavy workload, but leaving students' messages on read is not acceptable, especially for urgent matters. This happens regularly and has caused problems for students many times. We suggest creating a better communication system where students can submit requests and track their status more easily.
P'Vichy told us that TETET was not required if we already submitted other English test scores. However, based on the SIT website, the policy has changed and TETET is now required for graduation. Many fourth-year students missed the exam because we believed our previous English scores were enough. P'DJ, as many students have shared the same concerns about his behavior
- Unequal treatment, Female students and Thai students receive better treatment and more attention, which makes other students uncomfortable. most importantly, the clear pattern of flirting with his students is completely unacceptable and must be stopped immediately.
- Students who are close to P'DJ get special treatment, such as being excused for late attendance or receiving other advantages.
- P'DJ's position is unclear. Sometimes acting like a senior student, sometimes like a professor. This creates tension during activities. The commanding and controlling behavior feels more like a dictator than a teacher. P'Jo has a similar position but never creates these problems or makes students feel uncomfortable. suggesting that P'DJ should receive training on professional conduct and learn to treat all students fairly and respectfully. The current situation affects the learning environment negatively.

column4:
Important academic and opportunity-related information does not always reach Burmese students (or other international students) in a timely or clear manner. For example, information about the Taiwan internship or related programs was not well communicated, while students from other international majors had already been preparing since the previous semester. This information gap creates inequality in access to opportunities and leaves students unsure about whom to contact for guidance or clarification.
I hope the SIT International Relations office can be more proactive in sharing information about exchange programs and overseas internships. The Faculty of Engineering and Science has its own International Affairs office, which is very active in regularly posting and announcing overseas opportunities. As a 4th-year student from the old curriculum, in my perspective I‚Äôm judging based on (quality / attending one class session) and only on the knowledge gained in class, not outside the classroom. My opinions are as follows:

1. Some courses do not meet the needs of real-world work because they are outdated, such as CSC325, CSC340, and CSC319. In my view, these courses should teach more than just GUI development and restructuring. I think the content is quite old. To make Java more practically useful, it should involve building a full Desktop Application or doing a Big Data project instead.

2. Courses that should be hands-on ended up being mostly theoretical. For example, CSC220 was very disappointing for me in terms of learning networking. I believe this subject has huge potential for further development, but it felt like there was a lot of talk and not much substance. We pay almost 50,000 baht to sit in an old CB building without doing any concrete lab work, unlike other faculties that pay less but have proper networking workshops. Meanwhile, we just sit there, looking at each other, after paying tens of thousands more but receiving lower quality than other departments.

CSC325 was also disappointing. I believe this course still has potential and could offer much more. There was no project at all. Most of the time was spent grinding through SeedLab, documenting it, and then taking the final exam. In the end, there was no real continuation or application. I see this course as almost useful ‚Äî it was just missing a focus on quality, as it emphasized quantity of work instead.

3. There was a gap in coding practice. During Years 1‚Äì2, it was the most stressful period, but also the most beneficial for me. However, in Years 3‚Äì4, I felt like coding almost completely disappeared. It became very theory-heavy, with not much hands-on practice. I understand that this might be due to the reasons mentioned in points 1 and 2. I also feel that this may have already been improved in the new curriculum. Overall, though, I found the learning experience enjoyable during my time here.

column4:
Language and General Education Courses (LNG and GEN): These courses are not useful and waste a lot of time. Students with very high IELTS scores still have to take basic language classes, which doesn't make sense. Additionally, the grading standards are unclear and difficult to verify.
Programming Courses: The instructors are skilled and knowledgeable, which is good. However, the courses focus too much on fundamentals and theory. The practical application is very limited. Students have to learn and adapt a lot on their own to be ready for internships.
Need for More Specialized Elective Courses: The curriculum should offer more specialized track options. For example, UX/UI in course 105 could be a full elective course, but currently it only covers basic concepts that cannot be applied in real work. We would like to see courses such as Game Development with Unity, Advanced Power BI for Data Science
Other industry-relevant specialized topics
Courses 100/101 (Coursera ), 301, and 302: These courses waste time and do not measure any real CS skills or abilities. I don't understand the purpose of having them except to take time away from more necessary work.

Most of the courses were quite helpful. To name a few:
CSC209 Data Structures: While the sessions occasionally ran longer than scheduled, the content and the instructor were excellent. The instructor explained concepts clearly with ample examples. Although class times were sometimes flexible due to his responsibilities as the Department Dean, the material remained highly practical and valuable.
CSC105 Web Application Development: Some students felt this course only covered the basics, but I personally appreciated the approach. It encourages "learning how to learn." Instead of just following instructions, we were pushed to think for ourselves. This is essential for developing the skills needed to form original ideas and manage our own projects.
Overall, I think a score of 4 is appropriate, as the quality of the class is great but there is still room for improvement.

I got really high English test score. I really don‚Äôt understand why, us as an international program students, have to learn such a basic English concept of an elementary school grader level? Not only it‚Äôs not useful it‚Äôs also waste of my time and energy to attend all those courses In Jarah course, I don‚Äôt understand why LINE is consistently used as the main communication channel for assignments, class materials, and important course details. LINE has limited message history accessibility and is not a professional or reliable platform for managing academic information.
Using LINE for quick reminders or minor announcements is acceptable. But relying on it for all course-related communication is excessive and problematic. The faculty already provides proper platforms such as Microsoft Teams and CSCMS, which are designed for structured communication, assignment posting, and long-term record keeping.
Because information is frequently shared only through LINE chats, important details are often missed or lost, leading to confusion among students. Assignments communicated verbally in class, through chat messages, or by asking students to take notes are subjective and lack clarity. As a result, many students are uncertain about task requirements, deadlines, and expectations.
Assignments and course materials should be consistently posted on Microsoft Teams or CSCMS in a clear, concrete, and centralized manner. This would significantly reduce misunderstandings and help students manage their work more effectively.
column6: I don't understand why we have to learn basic English concepts that are at an elementary school level as part of our international program.

I understand that P'Nick has a heavy workload, but leaving students' messages on read is not acceptable, especially for urgent matters. This happens regularly and has caused problems for students many times. We suggest creating a better communication system where students can submit requests and track their status more easily.
P'Vichy told us that TETET was not required if we already submitted other English test scores. However, based on the SIT website, the policy has changed and TETET is now required for graduation. Many fourth-year students missed the exam because we believed our previous English scores were enough. P'DJ, as many students have shared the same concerns about his behavior
- Unequal treatment, Female students and Thai students receive better treatment and more attention, which makes other students uncomfortable. most importantly, the clear pattern of flirting with his students is completely unacceptable and must be stopped immediately.
- Students who are close to P'DJ get special treatment, such as being excused for late attendance or receiving other advantages.
- P'DJ's position is unclear. Sometimes acting like a senior student, sometimes like a professor. This creates tension during activities. The commanding and controlling behavior feels more like a dictator than a teacher. P'Jo has a similar position but never creates these problems or makes students feel uncomfortable. suggesting that P'DJ should receive training on professional conduct and learn to treat all students fairly and respectfully. The current situation affects the learning environment negatively.
column6: Leaving students' messages on read is not acceptable, especially for urgent matters, and a better communication system is needed.

column4:
Important academic and opportunity-related information does not always reach Burmese students (or other international students) in a timely or clear manner. For example, information about the Taiwan internship or related programs was not well communicated, while students from other international majors had already been preparing since the previous semester. This information gap creates inequality in access to opportunities and leaves students unsure about whom to contact for guidance or clarification.
I hope the SIT International Relations office can be more proactive in sharing information about exchange programs and overseas internships. The Faculty of Engineering and Science has its own International Affairs office, which is very active in regularly posting and announcing overseas opportunities. In comparison, SIT IR has been relatively quiet, and some students are not even aware that the office exists.
If workload or capacity is an issue, perhaps the university could consider hiring additional staff or involving student assistants to help with outreach and communication.
column6: Important academic and opportunity-related information does not always reach Burmese students (or other international students) in a timely or clear manner.

As a 4th-year student from the old curriculum, in my perspective I‚Äôm judging based on (quality / attending one class session) and only on the knowledge gained in class, not outside the classroom. My opinions are as follows:

1. Some courses do not meet the needs of real-world work because they are outdated, such as CSC325, CSC340, and CSC319. In my view, these courses should teach more than just GUI development and restructuring. I think the content is quite old. To make Java more practically useful, it should involve building a full Desktop Application or doing a Big Data project instead.

2. Courses that should be hands-on ended up being mostly theoretical. For example, CSC220 was very disappointing for me in terms of learning networking. I believe this subject has huge potential for further development, but it felt like there was a lot of talk and not much substance. We pay almost 50,000 baht to sit in an old CB building without doing any concrete lab work, unlike other faculties that pay less but have proper networking workshops. Meanwhile, we just sit there, looking at each other, after paying tens of thousands more but receiving lower quality than other departments.

CSC325 was also disappointing. I believe this course still has potential and could offer much more. There was no project at all. Most of the time was spent grinding through SeedLab, documenting it, and then taking the final exam. In the end, there was no real continuation or application. I see this course as almost useful ‚Äî it was just missing a focus on quality, as it emphasized quantity of work instead.

3. There was a gap in coding practice. During Years 1‚Äì2, it was the most stressful period, but also the most beneficial for me. However, in Years 3‚Äì4, I felt like coding almost completely disappeared. It became very theory-heavy, with not much hands-on practice. I understand that this might be due to the reasons mentioned in points 1 and 2. I also feel that this may have already been improved in the new curriculum. Overall, though, I found the learning experience enjoyable during my time here.

column4:
Language and General Education Courses (LNG and GEN): These courses are not useful and waste a lot of time. Students with very high IELTS scores still have to take basic language classes, which doesn't make sense. Additionally, the grading standards are unclear and difficult to verify.
Programming Courses: The instructors are skilled and knowledgeable, which is good. However, the courses focus too much on fundamentals and theory. The practical application is very limited. Students have to learn and adapt a lot on their own to be ready for internships.
Need for More Specialized Elective Courses: The curriculum should offer more specialized track options. For example, UX/UI in course 105 could be a full elective course, but currently it only covers basic concepts that cannot be applied in real work. We would like to see courses such as Game Development with Unity, Advanced Power BI for Data Science
Other industry-relevant specialized topics
Courses 100/101 (Coursera ), 301, and 302: These courses waste time and do not measure any real CS skills or abilities. I don't understand the purpose of having them except to take time away from more necessary work.

I got really high English test score. I really don‚Äôt understand why, us as an international program students, have to learn such a basic English concept of an elementary school grader level? Not only it‚Äôs not useful it‚Äôs also waste of my time and energy to attend all those courses In Jarah course, I don‚Äôt understand why LINE is consistently used as the main communication channel for assignments, class materials, and important course details. LINE has limited message history accessibility and is not a professional or reliable platform for managing academic information.
Using LINE for quick reminders or minor announcements is acceptable. But relying on it for all course-related communication is excessive and problematic. The faculty already provides proper platforms such as Microsoft Teams and CSCMS, which are designed for structured communication, assignment posting, and long-term record keeping.
Because information is frequently shared only through LINE chats, important details are often missed or lost, leading to confusion among students. For example, information about the Taiwan internship or related programs was not well communicated, while students from other international majors had already been preparing since the previous semester. This information gap creates inequality in access to opportunities and leaves students unsure about whom to contact for guidance or clarification.
I hope the SIT International Relations office can be more proactive in sharing information about exchange programs and overseas internships. The Faculty of Engineering and Science has its own International Affairs office, which is very active in regularly posting and announcing overseas opportunities. In comparison, SIT IR has been relatively quiet, and some students are not even aware that the office exists.
If workload or capacity is an issue, perhaps the university could consider hiring additional staff or involving student assistants to help with outreach and communication.

As a 4th-year student from the old curriculum, in my perspective I‚Äôm judging based on (quality / attending one class session) and only on the knowledge gained in class, not outside the classroom. My opinions are as follows:

1. Some courses do not meet the needs of real-world work because they are outdated, such as CSC325, CSC340, and CSC319. In my view, these courses should teach more than just GUI development and restructuring. I think the content is quite old. To make Java more practically useful, it should involve building a full Desktop Application or doing a Big Data project instead.

2. Courses that should be hands-on ended up being mostly theoretical. For example, CSC220 was very disappointing for me in terms of learning networking. I believe this subject has huge potential for further development, but it felt like there was a lot of talk and not much substance. We pay almost 50,000 baht to sit in an old CB building without doing any concrete lab work, unlike other faculties that pay less but have proper networking workshops. Meanwhile, we just sit there, looking at each other, after paying tens of thousands more but receiving lower quality than other departments.

CSC325 was also disappointing. I believe this course still has potential and could offer much more. There was no project at all. Most of the time was spent grinding through SeedLab, documenting it, and then taking the final exam. In the end, there was no real continuation or application. I see this course as almost useful ‚Äî it was just missing a focus on quality, as it emphasized quantity of work instead.

3. There was a gap in coding practice. During Years 1‚Äì2, it was the most stressful period, but also the most beneficial for me. However, in Years 3‚Äì4, I felt like coding almost completely disappeared. It became very theory-heavy, with not much hands-on practice. I understand that this might be due to the reasons mentioned in points 1 and 2. I also feel that this may have already been improved in the new curriculum. Overall, though, I found the learning experience enjoyable during my time here.

column4:
Language and General Education Courses (LNG and GEN): These courses are not useful and waste a lot of time. Students with very high IELTS scores still have to take basic language classes, which doesn't make sense. Additionally, the grading standards are unclear and difficult to verify.
Programming Courses: The instructors are skilled and knowledgeable, which is good. However, the courses focus too much on fundamentals and theory. The practical application is very limited. Students have to learn and adapt a lot on their own to be ready for internships.
Need for More Specialized Elective Courses: The curriculum should offer more specialized track options. For example, UX/UI in course 105 could be a full elective course, but currently it only covers basic concepts that cannot be applied in real work. We would like to see courses such as Game Development with Unity, Advanced Power BI for Data Science
Other industry-relevant specialized topics
Courses 100/101 (Coursera ), 301, and 302: These courses waste time and do not measure any real CS skills or abilities. I don't understand the purpose of having them except to take time away from more necessary work.
column6: I think Language and General Education Courses (LNG and GEN) are not useful and waste a lot of time.

Most of the courses were quite helpful. To name a few:
CSC209 Data Structures: While the sessions occasionally ran longer than scheduled, the content and the instructor were excellent. The instructor explained concepts clearly with ample examples. Although class times were sometimes flexible due to his responsibilities as the Department Dean, the material remained highly practical and valuable.
CSC105 Web Application Development: Some students felt this course only covered the basics, but I personally appreciated the approach. It encourages "learning how to learn." Instead of just following instructions, we were pushed to think for ourselves. This is essential for developing the skills needed to form original ideas and manage our own projects.
Overall, I think a score of 4 is appropriate, as the quality of the class is great but there is still room for improvement.

I got really high English test score. I really don‚Äôt understand why, us as an international program students, have to learn such a basic English concept of an elementary school grader level? Not only it‚Äôs not useful it‚Äôs also waste of my time and energy to attend all those courses In Jarah course, I don‚Äôt understand why LINE is consistently used as the main communication channel for assignments, class materials, and important course details. LINE has limited message history accessibility and is not a professional or reliable platform for managing academic information.
Using LINE for quick reminders or minor announcements is acceptable. But relying on it for all course-related communication is excessive and problematic. The faculty already provides proper platforms such as Microsoft Teams and CSCMS, which are designed for structured communication, assignment posting, and long-term record keeping.
Because information is frequently shared only through LINE chats, important details are often missed or lost, leading to confusion among students. Assignments communicated verbally in class, through chat messages, or by asking students to take notes are subjective and lack clarity. As a result, many students are uncertain about task requirements, deadlines, and expectations.
Assignments and course materials should be consistently posted on Microsoft Teams or CSCMS in a clear, concrete, and centralized manner. This would significantly reduce misunderstandings and help students manage their work more effectively.
column6: I don't understand why we have to learn basic English concepts that are at an elementary school level as part of our international program.

The Faculty of Engineering and Science has its own International Affairs office, which is very active in regularly posting and announcing overseas opportunities. In comparison, SIT IR has been relatively quiet, and some students are not even aware that the office exists.

As a 4th-year student from the old curriculum, in my perspective I‚Äôm judging based on (quality / attending one class session) and only on the knowledge gained in class, not outside the classroom. My opinions are as follows:

1. Some courses do not meet the needs of real-world work because they are outdated, such as CSC325, CSC340, and CSC319. In my view, these courses should teach more than just GUI development and restructuring. I think the content is quite old. To make Java more practically useful, it should involve building a full Desktop Application or doing a Big Data project instead.

2. Courses that should be hands-on ended up being mostly theoretical. For example, CSC220 was very disappointing for me in terms of learning networking. I believe this subject has huge potential for further development, but it felt like there was a lot of talk and not much substance. We pay almost 50,000 baht to sit in an old CB building without doing any concrete lab work, unlike other faculties that pay less but have proper networking workshops. Meanwhile, we just sit there, looking at each other, after paying tens of thousands more but receiving lower quality than other departments.

CSC325 was also disappointing. I believe this course still has potential and could offer much more. There was no project at all. Most of the time was spent grinding through SeedLab, documenting it, and then taking the final exam. In the end, there was no real continuation or application. I see this course as almost useful ‚Äî it was just missing a focus on quality, as it emphasized quantity of work instead.

3. There was a gap in coding practice. During Years 1‚Äì2, it was the most stressful period, but also the most beneficial for me. However, in Years 3‚Äì4, I felt like coding almost completely disappeared. It became very theory-heavy, with not much hands-on practice. I understand that this might be due to the reasons mentioned in points 1 and 2. I also feel that this may have already been improved in the new curriculum. Overall, though, I found the learning experience enjoyable during my time here.

column4:
Language and General Education Courses (LNG and GEN): These courses are not useful and waste a lot of time. Students with very high IELTS scores still have to take basic language classes, which doesn't make sense. Additionally, the grading standards are unclear and difficult to verify.
Programming Courses: The instructors are skilled and knowledgeable, which is good. However, the courses focus too much on fundamentals and theory. The practical application is very limited. Students have to learn and adapt a lot on their own to be ready for internships.
Need for More Specialized Elective Courses: The curriculum should offer more specialized track options. For example, UX/UI in course 105 could be a full elective course, but currently it only covers basic concepts that cannot be applied in real work. We would like to see courses such as Game Development with Unity, Advanced Power BI for Data Science
Other industry-relevant specialized topics
Courses 100/101 (Coursera ), 301, and 302: These courses waste time and do not measure any real CS skills or abilities. I don't understand the purpose of having them except to take time away from more necessary work.
column6: I think Language and General Education Courses (LNG and GEN) are not useful and waste a lot of time.

Most of the courses were quite helpful. To name a few:
CSC209 Data Structures: While the sessions occasionally ran longer than scheduled, the content and the instructor were excellent. The instructor explained concepts clearly with ample examples. Although class times were sometimes flexible due to his responsibilities as the Department Dean, the material remained highly practical and valuable.
CSC105 Web Application Development: Some students felt this course only covered the basics, but I personally appreciated the approach. It encourages "learning how to learn." Instead of just following instructions, we were pushed to think for ourselves. This is essential for developing the skills needed to form original ideas and manage our own projects.
Overall, I think a score of 4 is appropriate, as the quality of the class is great but there is still room for improvement.

I got really high English test score. I really don‚Äôt understand why, us as an international program students, have to learn such a basic English concept of an elementary school grader level? Not only it‚Äôs not useful it‚Äôs also waste of my time and energy to attend all those courses In Jarah course, I don‚Äôt understand why LINE is consistently used as the main communication channel for assignments, class materials, and important course details. LINE has limited message history accessibility and is not a professional or reliable platform for managing academic information.
Using LINE for quick reminders or minor announcements is acceptable. But relying on it for all course-related communication is excessive and problematic. The faculty already provides proper platforms such as Microsoft Teams and CSCMS, which are designed for structured communication, assignment posting, and long-term record keeping.
Because information is frequently shared only through LINE chats, important details are often missed or lost, leading to confusion among students. Assignments communicated verbally in class, through chat messages, or by asking students to take notes are subjective and lack clarity. As a result, many students are uncertain about task requirements, deadlines, and expectations.
Assignments and course materials should be consistently posted on Microsoft Teams or CSCMS in a clear, concrete, and centralized manner. This would significantly reduce misunderstandings and help students manage their work more effectively.
column6: I don't understand why we have to learn basic English concepts that are at an elementary school level.

column4:
Important academic and opportunity-related information does not always reach Burmese students (or other international students) in a timely or clear manner. For example, information about the Taiwan internship or related programs was not well communicated, while students from other international majors had already been preparing since the previous semester. This information gap creates inequality in access to opportunities and leaves students unsure about whom to contact for guidance or clarification.
I hope the SIT International Relations office can be more proactive in sharing information about exchange programs and overseas internships. The Faculty of Engineering and Science has its own International Affairs office, which is very active in regularly posting and announcing overseas opportunities. In comparison, SIT IR has been relatively quiet, and some students are not even aware that the office exists.
If workload or capacity is an issue, perhaps the university could consider hiring additional staff or involving student assistants to help with outreach and communication.

As a 4th-year student from the old curriculum, in my perspective I‚Äôm judging based on (quality / attending one class session) and only on the knowledge gained in class, not outside the classroom. My opinions are as follows:

1. Some courses do not meet the needs of real-world work because they are outdated, such as CSC325, CSC340, and CSC319. In my view, these courses should teach more than just GUI development and restructuring. I think the content is quite old. To make Java more practically useful, it should involve building a full Desktop Application or doing a Big Data project instead.

2. Courses that should be hands-on ended up being mostly theoretical. For example, CSC220 was very disappointing for me in terms of learning networking. I believe this subject has huge potential for further development, but it felt like there was a lot of talk and not much substance. We pay almost 50,000 baht to sit in an old CB building without doing any concrete lab work, unlike other faculties that pay less but have proper networking workshops. Meanwhile, we just sit there, looking at each other, after paying tens of thousands more but receiving lower quality than other departments.

CSC325 was also disappointing. I believe this course still has potential and could offer much more. There was no project at all. Most of the time was spent grinding through SeedLab, documenting it, and then taking the final exam. In the end, there was no real continuation or application. I see this course as almost useful ‚Äî it was just missing a focus on quality, as it emphasized quantity of work instead.

3. There was a gap in coding practice. During Years 1‚Äì2, it was the most stressful period, but also the most beneficial for me. However, in Years 3‚Äì4, I felt like coding almost completely disappeared. It became very theory-heavy, with not much hands-on practice. I understand that this might be due to the reasons mentioned in points 1 and 2. I also feel that this may have already been improved in the new curriculum. Overall, though, I found the learning experience enjoyable during my time here.

column4:
Language and General Education Courses (LNG and GEN): These courses are not useful and waste a lot of time. Students with very high IELTS scores still have to take basic language classes, which doesn't make sense. Additionally, the grading standards are unclear and difficult to verify.
Programming Courses: The instructors are skilled and knowledgeable, which is good. However, the courses focus too much on fundamentals and theory. The practical application is very limited. Students have to learn and adapt a lot on their own to be ready for internships.
Need for More Specialized Elective Courses: The curriculum should offer more specialized track options. For example, UX/UI in course 105 could be a full elective course, but currently it only covers basic concepts that cannot be applied in real work. We would like to see courses such as Game Development with Unity, Advanced Power BI for Data Science
Other industry-relevant specialized topics
Courses 100/101 (Coursera ), 301, and 302: These courses waste time and do not measure any real CS skills or abilities. I don't understand the purpose of having them except to take time away from more necessary work.
column6: I think Language and General Education Courses (LNG and GEN) are not useful and waste a lot of time.

Most of the courses were quite helpful. To name a few:
CSC209 Data Structures: While the sessions occasionally ran longer than scheduled, the content and the instructor were excellent. The instructor explained concepts clearly with ample examples. Although class times were sometimes flexible due to his responsibilities as the Department Dean, the material remained highly practical and valuable.
CSC105 Web Application Development: Some students felt this course only covered the basics, but I personally appreciated the approach. It encourages "learning how to learn." Instead of just following instructions, we were pushed to think for ourselves. This is essential for developing the skills needed to form original ideas and manage our own projects.
Overall, I think a score of 4 is appropriate, as the quality of the class is great but there is still room for improvement.

I got really high English test score. I really don‚Äôt understand why, us as an international program students, have to learn such a basic English concept of an elementary school grader level? Not only it‚Äôs not useful it‚Äôs also waste of my time and energy to attend all those courses In Jarah course, I don‚Äôt understand why LINE is consistently used as the main communication channel for assignments, class materials, and important course details. LINE has limited message history accessibility and is not a professional or reliable platform for managing academic information.
Using LINE for quick reminders or minor announcements is acceptable. But relying on it for all course-related communication is excessive and problematic. The faculty already provides proper platforms such as Microsoft Teams and CSCMS, which are designed for structured communication, assignment posting, and long-term record keeping.
Because information is frequently shared only through LINE chats, important details are often missed or lost, leading to confusion among students. Assignments communicated verbally in class, through chat messages, or by asking students to take notes are subjective and lack clarity. As a result, many students are uncertain about task requirements, deadlines, and expectations.
Assignments and course materials should be consistently posted on Microsoft Teams or CSCMS in a clear, concrete, and centralized manner. This would significantly reduce misunderstandings and help students manage their work more effectively.
column6: I don't understand why we have to learn basic English concepts that are at an elementary school level.

Important academic and opportunity-related information does not always reach Burmese students (or other international students) in a timely or clear manner. For example, information about the Taiwan internship or related programs was not well communicated, while students from other international majors had already been preparing since the previous semester. This information gap creates inequality in access to opportunities and leaves students unsure about whom to contact for guidance or clarification.
I hope the SIT International Relations office can be more proactive in sharing information about exchange programs and overseas internships. The Faculty of Engineering and Science has its own International Affairs office, which is very active in regularly posting and announcing overseas opportunities. In comparison, SIT IR has been relatively quiet, and some students are not even aware that the office exists.
If workload or capacity is an issue, perhaps the university could consider hiring additional staff or involving student assistants to help with outreach and communication.

column4:
As a 4th-year student from the old curriculum, in my perspective I‚Äôm judging based on (quality / attending one class session) and only on the knowledge gained in class, not outside the classroom. My opinions are as follows:

1. Some courses do not meet the needs of real-world work because they are outdated, such as CSC325, CSC340, and CSC319. In my view, these courses should teach more than just GUI development and restructuring. I think the content is quite old. To make Java more practically useful, it should involve building a full Desktop Application or doing a Big Data project instead.

2. Courses that should be hands-on ended up being mostly theoretical. For example, CSC220 was very disappointing for me in terms of learning networking. I believe this subject has huge potential for further development, but it felt like there was a lot of talk and not much substance. We pay almost 50,000 baht to sit in an old CB building without doing any concrete lab work, unlike other faculties that pay less but have proper networking workshops. Meanwhile, we just sit there, looking at each other, after paying tens of thousands more but receiving lower quality than other departments.

CSC325 was also disappointing. I believe this course still has potential and could offer much more. There was no project at all. Most of the time was spent grinding through SeedLab, documenting it, and then taking the final exam. In the end, there was no real continuation or application. I see this course as almost useful ‚Äî it was just missing a focus on quality, as it emphasized quantity of work instead.

3. There was a gap in coding practice. During Years 1‚Äì2, it was the most stressful period, but also the most beneficial for me. However, in Years 3‚Äì4, I felt like coding almost completely disappeared. It became very theory-heavy, with not much hands-on practice. I understand that this might be due to the reasons mentioned in points 1 and 2. I also feel that this may have already been improved in the new curriculum. Overall, though, I found the learning experience enjoyable during my time here.

Language and General Education Courses (LNG and GEN): These courses are not useful and waste a lot of time. Students with very high IELTS scores still have to take basic language classes, which doesn't make sense. Additionally, the grading standards are unclear and difficult to verify.
Programming Courses: The instructors are skilled and knowledgeable, which is good. However, the courses focus too much on fundamentals and theory. The practical application is very limited. Students have to learn and adapt a lot on their own to be ready for internships.

For example, UX/UI in course 105 could be a full elective course, but currently it only covers basic concepts that cannot be applied in real work. Other industry-relevant specialized topics

Most of the courses were quite helpful. To name a few:
CSC209 Data Structures: While the sessions occasionally ran longer than scheduled, the content and the instructor were excellent. The instructor explained concepts clearly with ample examples. Instead of just following instructions, we were pushed to think for ourselves. This is essential for developing the skills needed to form original ideas and manage our own projects.
Overall, I think a score of 4 is appropriate, as the quality of the class is great but there is still room for improvement.

I got really high English test score. I really don‚Äôt understand why, us as an international program students, have to learn such a basic English concept of an elementary school grader level? Not only it‚Äôs not useful it‚Äôs also waste of my time and energy to attend all those courses In Jarah course, I don‚Äôt understand why LINE is consistently used as the main communication channel for assignments, class materials, and important course details. LINE has limited message history accessibility and is not a professional or reliable platform for managing academic information.
Using LINE for quick reminders or minor announcements is acceptable. But relying on it for all course-related communication is excessive and problematic. The faculty already provides proper platforms such as Microsoft Teams and CSCMS, which are designed for structured communication, assignment posting, and long-term record keeping.
Because information is frequently shared only through LINE chats, important details are often missed or lost, leading to confusion among students. Assignments communicated verbally in class, through chat messages, or by asking students to take notes are subjective and lack clarity. As a result, many students are uncertain about task requirements, deadlines, and expectations.
Assignments and course materials should be consistently posted on Microsoft Teams or CSCMS in a clear, concrete, and centralized manner. This would significantly reduce misunderstandings and help students manage their work more effectively.
column6: I don't understand why we have to learn basic English concepts that are at an elementary school level.

I understand that P'Nick has a heavy workload, but leaving students' messages on read is not acceptable, especially for urgent matters. This happens regularly and has caused problems for students many times. We suggest creating a better communication system where students can submit requests and track their status more easily.

- P'DJ's position is unclear. Sometimes acting like a senior student, sometimes like a professor. This creates tension during activities. The commanding and controlling behavior feels more like a dictator than a teacher. P'Jo has a similar position but never creates these problems or makes students feel uncomfortable. suggesting that P'DJ should receive training on professional conduct and learn to treat all students fairly and respectfully. The current situation affects the learning environment negatively.

column4:
Important academic and opportunity-related information does not always reach Burmese students (or other international students) in a timely or clear manner. For example, information about the Taiwan internship or related programs was not well communicated, while students from other international majors had already been preparing since the previous semester. This information gap creates inequality in access to opportunities and leaves students unsure about whom to contact for guidance or clarification.
I hope the SIT International Relations office can be more proactive in sharing information about exchange programs and overseas internships. The Faculty of Engineering and Science has its own International Affairs office, which is very active in regularly posting and announcing overseas opportunities. In comparison, SIT IR has been relatively quiet, and some students are not even aware that the office exists.
If workload or capacity is an issue, perhaps the university could consider hiring additional staff or involving student assistants to help with outreach and communication.

column4:
As a 4th-year student from the old curriculum, in my perspective I‚Äôm judging based on (quality / attending one class session) and only on the knowledge gained in class, not outside the classroom. My opinions are as follows:

1. Some courses do not meet the needs of real-world work because they are outdated, such as CSC325, CSC340, and CSC319. In my view, these courses should teach more than just GUI development and restructuring. I think the content is quite old. column4:
Language and General Education Courses (LNG and GEN): These courses are not useful and waste a lot of time. Students with very high IELTS scores still have to take basic language classes, which doesn't make sense. Additionally, the grading standards are unclear and difficult to verify.
Programming Courses: The instructors are skilled and knowledgeable, which is good. However, the courses focus too much on fundamentals and theory. The practical application is very limited. Students have to learn and adapt a lot on their own to be ready for internships.
Need for More Specialized Elective Courses: The curriculum should offer more specialized track options. For example, UX/UI in course 105 could be a full elective course, but currently it only covers basic concepts that cannot be applied in real work. We would like to see courses such as Game Development with Unity, Advanced Power BI for Data Science
Other industry-relevant specialized topics
Courses 100/101 (Coursera ), 301, and 302: These courses waste time and do not measure any real CS skills or abilities. I don't understand the purpose of having them except to take time away from more necessary work.

Most of the courses were quite helpful. To name a few:
CSC209 Data Structures: While the sessions occasionally ran longer than scheduled, the content and the instructor were excellent. The instructor explained concepts clearly with ample examples. Although class times were sometimes flexible due to his responsibilities as the Department Dean, the material remained highly practical and valuable.
CSC105 Web Application Development: Some students felt this course only covered the basics, but I personally appreciated the approach. It encourages "learning how to learn." Instead of just following instructions, we were pushed to think for ourselves. This is essential for developing the skills needed to form original ideas and manage our own projects.
Overall, I think a score of 4 is appropriate, as the quality of the class is great but there is still room for improvement.

I got really high English test score. I really don‚Äôt understand why, us as an international program students, have to learn such a basic English concept of an elementary school grader level? Not only it‚Äôs not useful it‚Äôs also waste of my time and energy to attend all those courses In Jarah course, I don‚Äôt understand why LINE is consistently used as the main communication channel for assignments, class materials, and important course details. LINE has limited message history accessibility and is not a professional or reliable platform for managing academic information.
Using LINE for quick reminders or minor announcements is acceptable. But relying on it for all course-related communication is excessive and problematic. The faculty already provides proper platforms such as Microsoft Teams and CSCMS, which are designed for structured communication, assignment posting, and long-term record keeping.
Because information is frequently shared only through LINE chats, important details are often missed or lost, leading to confusion among students. Assignments communicated verbally in class, through chat messages, or by asking students to take notes are subjective and lack clarity. As a result, many students are uncertain about task requirements, deadlines, and expectations.
Assignments and course materials should be consistently posted on Microsoft Teams or CSCMS in a clear, concrete, and centralized manner. This would significantly reduce misunderstandings and help students manage their work more effectively.

I understand that P'Nick has a heavy workload, but leaving students' messages on read is not acceptable, especially for urgent matters. This happens regularly and has caused problems for students many times. We suggest creating a better communication system where students can submit requests and track their status more easily.
P'Vichy told us that TETET was not required if we already submitted other English test scores. However, based on the SIT website, the policy has changed and TETET is now required for graduation. Many fourth-year students missed the exam because we believed our previous English scores were enough. P'DJ, as many students have shared the same concerns about his behavior
- Unequal treatment, Female students and Thai students receive better treatment and more attention, which makes other students uncomfortable. most importantly, the clear pattern of flirting with his students is completely unacceptable and must be stopped immediately.
- Students who are close to P'DJ get special treatment, such as being excused for late attendance or receiving other advantages.
- P'DJ's position is unclear. Sometimes acting like a senior student, sometimes like a professor. This creates tension during activities. The commanding and controlling behavior feels more like a dictator than a teacher. P'Jo has a similar position but never creates these problems or makes students feel uncomfortable. suggesting that P'DJ should receive training on professional conduct and learn to treat all students fairly and respectfully. The current situation affects the learning environment negatively.

column4:
Important academic and opportunity-related information does not always reach Burmese students (or other international students) in a timely or clear manner. For example, information about the Taiwan internship or related programs was not well communicated, while students from other international majors had already been preparing since the previous semester. This information gap creates inequality in access to opportunities and leaves students unsure about whom to contact for guidance or clarification.
I hope the SIT International Relations office can be more proactive in sharing information about exchange programs and overseas internships. The Faculty of Engineering and Science has its own International Affairs office, which is very active in regularly posting and announcing overseas opportunities. In comparison, SIT IR has been relatively quiet, and some students are not even aware that the office exists.
If workload or capacity is an issue, perhaps the university could consider hiring additional staff or involving student assistants to help with outreach and communication.

column4:
As a 4th-year student from the old curriculum, in my perspective I‚Äôm judging based on (quality / attending one class session) and only on the knowledge gained in class, not outside the classroom. My opinions are as follows:

1. Some courses do not meet the needs of real-world work because they are outdated, such as CSC325, CSC340, and CSC319. In my view, these courses should teach more than just GUI development and restructuring. I think the content is quite old. To make Java more practically useful, it should involve building a full Desktop Application or doing a Big Data project instead.

2. Courses that should be hands-on ended up being mostly theoretical. For example, CSC220 was very disappointing for me in terms of learning networking. I believe this subject has huge potential for further development, but it felt like there was a lot of talk and not much substance. We pay almost 50,000 baht to sit in an old CB building without doing any concrete lab work, unlike other faculties that pay less but have proper networking workshops. Meanwhile, we just sit there, looking at each other, after paying tens of thousands more but receiving lower quality than other departments.

CSC325 was also disappointing. I believe this course still has potential and could offer much more. There was no project at all. Most of the time was spent grinding through SeedLab, documenting it, and then taking the final exam. In the end, there was no real continuation or application. I see this course as almost useful ‚Äî it was just missing a focus on quality, as it emphasized quantity of work instead.

3. There was a gap in coding practice. During Years 1‚Äì2, it was the most stressful period, but also the most beneficial for me. However, in Years 3‚Äì4, I felt like coding almost completely disappeared. It became very theory-heavy, with not much hands-on practice. I understand that this might be due to the reasons mentioned in points 1 and 2. I also feel that this may have already been improved in the new curriculum. Overall, though, I found the learning experience enjoyable during my time here.

column4:
Language and General Education Courses (LNG and GEN): These courses are not useful and waste a lot of time. Students with very high IELTS scores still have to take basic language classes, which doesn't make sense. Additionally, the grading standards are unclear and difficult to verify.
Programming Courses: The instructors are skilled and knowledgeable, which is good. However, the courses focus too much on fundamentals and theory. The practical application is very limited. Students have to learn and adapt a lot on their own to be ready for internships.

I got really high English test score. I really don‚Äôt understand why, us as an international program students, have to learn such a basic English concept of an elementary school grader level? Not only it‚Äôs not useful it‚Äôs also waste of my time and energy to attend all those courses In Jarah course, I don‚Äôt understand why LINE is consistently used as the main communication channel for assignments, class materials, and important course details. LINE has limited message history accessibility and is not a professional or reliable platform for managing academic information.
Using LINE for quick reminders or minor announcements is acceptable. But relying on it for all course-related communication is excessive and problematic. The faculty already provides proper platforms such as Microsoft Teams and CSCMS, which are designed for structured communication, assignment posting, and long-term record keeping.
Because information is frequently shared only through LINE chats, important details are often missed or lost, leading to confusion among students. Assignments communicated verbally in class, through chat messages, or by asking students to take notes are subjective and lack clarity. As a result, many students are uncertain about task requirements, deadlines, and expectations.
Assignments and course materials should be consistently posted on Microsoft Teams or CSCMS in a clear, concrete, and centralized manner. This would significantly reduce misunderstandings and help students manage their work more effectively.

Scholarship Limitations:
Scholarships have too many restrictions for Thai students, and the Academic Award amount decreases every year. This is very disappointing, as many students rely on this financial support.
International Student Support:
Moving to a foreign country is already difficult. I hope the faculty can make us feel warm and safe by building a stronger community for international students.
Internship Support:
The faculty needs to provide much more support for internships. Jobs for international students are very rare and often pay less than positions for Thai students. I would like to see partnerships similar to those in the Engineering faculty to make finding internships easier.

column4:
Important academic and opportunity-related information does not always reach Burmese students (or other international students) in a timely or clear manner. For example, information about the Taiwan internship or related programs was not well communicated, while students from other international majors had already been preparing since the previous semester. This information gap creates inequality in access to opportunities and leaves students unsure about whom to contact for guidance or clarification.
I hope the SIT International Relations office can be more proactive in sharing information about exchange programs and overseas internships. The Faculty of Engineering and Science has its own International Affairs office, which is very active in regularly posting and announcing overseas opportunities. In comparison, SIT IR has been relatively quiet, and some students are not even aware that the office exists.
If workload or capacity is an issue, perhaps the university could consider hiring additional staff or involving student assistants to help with outreach and communication.
